reasons: Both find the off-by-one, trace the negative-start boundary cases correctly, and propose a fix that returns exactly n items, so the rubric separates them not at all. B wins on precision: it names the single root cause (a negative slice start counts from the end instead of clamping), its one-expression fix handles n = 0, n >= len and negative n without a branch, and its warning about the tempting items[-n:] at n = 0 is exactly right. A is broader (executable asserts, a deque note for iterators) but misdescribes its own branchless alternative as usable only when n <= 0 cannot occur, when items[max(len(items) - n, 0):] already returns [] there.

A: Presents items[max(len(items) - n, 0):] as valid only if n <= 0 is impossible by contract; that expression in fact returns [] for n = 0 and for negative n, so no such precondition is needed.
